result: Of the god Agni, सुभगस्य (*subhagasya*) — of good wealth, one who is to be well resorted to — the संदृक् (*saṃdṛk*) (sight, glance) is श्रेष्ठा (*śreṣṭhā*), exceedingly praiseworthy; among mortals it is चित्रतमा (*citratamā*), most to be honoured and worshipped, and it is स्पार्हा (*spārhā*), to be desired by all. An illustration follows. As, for a man who desires milk, the शुचि (*śuci*) (bright, full of splendour) घृतं (*ghṛtaṃ*), the heated (तप्तं (*taptaṃ*)) milk of the अघ्न्या (*aghnyā*) cow that flows forth, is desirable; ⟨NOTE:345⟩ so too the sight is desired. There is a second illustration: as, for a mortal begging for a cow, the मंहना (*maṃhanā*) of a milch cow — मंहति (*maṃhati*) is a root meaning giving — ⟨NOTE:346⟩ that is, as a gift is pleasing, so is it. The rest gives accent and derivation of सुभगस्य (*subhagasya*), स्मार्हा (*smārhā*) and देवस्य (*devasya*) (Grammar section).

result: The word न (*na*) in this ṛk does not have the sense of comparison; it has the sense of "now" (samprati). Just as the word iha means "here", yet the sentence इहैव निधेहि (*ihaiva nidhehi*) means "put it now", so it should be understood. Therefore the phrase यावन्मात्रमुषसो न प्रतीकं (*yāvanmātramuṣaso na pratīkaṃ*) ⟨NOTE:407⟩ means: for as long as, that is, for how long (only a short time) the dawn-time at the end of the night spreads, for just so long. The sentence सुपर्ण्यः सुपतना एता रात्रयो वसते मातरिश्वन (*suparṇyaḥ supatanā etā rātrayo vasate mātariśvana*) means: O Mātariśvan, the birds of fine wings, flying, hold the dawn-time. That is, "birds" here means the nights. The word suparṇyaḥ which indicates this, meaning "of various wings", conveys the sense of the various (fine) colours of the dawn-time. Therefore suparṇyaḥ means that when Uṣas rises at the end of the night, that Uṣas has various or beautiful colours. The extent of this dawn-time is very small. Since sunrise follows very quickly after the dawn-time, the dawn-time is very small in extent: the intention is, only for a very short time. The human hotṛ is inferior to Agni, the divine hotṛ; therefore the brāhmaṇa, the human hotṛ, seated in a place lower than Agni installed on the sacrificial altar, performs the hotṛ's work only for a very short time, by the grace of Agni, who is of special wisdom: this is the main intention. By this the smallness of man and the greatness of Agni become evident. Since this ṛk says that the brāhmaṇa, the human hotṛ, seated on the sacrificial altar, performs the hotṛ's work praising Agni, the divine hotṛ, it is clearly evident that here Vaiśvānara Agni means the earthly Agni who is praised, and not the Āditya.

result: Sāyaṇa says: anirena: ira is food; by speech devoid of it; phalgyena ⟨NOTE:412⟩; pratītyena, "to be approached", that is, "to be climbed" (ārohya); kṛdhunā, "short": kṛdhu is a name for "short", as the lists of its names show (कृधुको वम्रक इति (*kṛdhuko vamraka iti*)). By speech of such kind, unsatisfied (atṛpāsaḥ) people, now (adha) here in this world, O Agni, what do they say to you? By speech without oblation nothing is obtained, that is the sense. But anāyudhāsaḥ: the word āyudha stands for a means; those devoid of means such as oblations, let them meet with asat, that is, with suffering (sacantām, "let them come together").
